cls: Cardioselective (beta-1) adrenergic receptor antagonist (beta-blocker); oral antihypertensive and ophthalmic anti-glaucoma agent
pharm: Selectively blocks beta-1 adrenoceptors, lowering blood pressure (oral) and reducing aqueous humour production to lower intraocular pressure (ophthalmic)
tags: Two forms: oral tablets (hypertension) and ophthalmic drops (glaucoma/ocular hypertension)
Cardioselective beta-1 blocker (relatively low membrane-stabilising / no ISA)
Caution in heart block, bradycardia, decompensated heart failure
Ophthalmic drops are systemically absorbed - same beta-blocker cautions apply
quick: Oral (HTN): 10 mg once daily, may increase to 20 mg after 7-14 days; Ophthalmic: 1 drop in affected eye(s) twice daily
Tablets: take consistently with or without food once daily; eye drops independent of meals
Use only if clearly needed; beta-blockers may cause fetal bradycardia / growth effects
Betaxolol passes into milk; monitor infant for bradycardia / hypoglycaemia
Oral: reduce dose in severe renal impairment / dialysis (e.g. start 5 mg/day)
Use with caution; consider lower starting oral dose
May enhance blood-pressure lowering / dizziness; use moderately
Heart rate and blood pressure (oral); intraocular pressure (ophthalmic); signs of heart failure
summary: Betaxolol is a cardioselective (beta-1) adrenergic receptor antagonist without significant intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and with little membrane-stabilising activity. It exists in two formulations. The ORAL tablet is indicated for the management of hypertension, alone or with other agents (particularly thiazide diuretics); the usual starting dose is 10 mg once daily, increased to 20 mg after 7-14 days if needed (doses above 20 mg add little antihypertensive effect). The OPHTHALMIC suspension/solution is indicated for elevated intraocular pressure in chronic open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension; the dose is one drop in the affected eye(s) twice daily. Topical ocular betaxolol is absorbed systemically, so the same beta-blocker precautions apply. As a beta-blocker it should not be stopped abruptly (risk of rebound angina, MI, or hypertension), and it is contraindicated in sinus bradycardia, AV block greater than first degree, cardiogenic shock, and overt cardiac failure. It can mask signs of hypoglycaemia and hyperthyroidism.
indications: Management of hypertension, alone or with other antihypertensive agents (oral tablet)
Treatment of elevated intraocular pressure in chronic open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension (ophthalmic)

dosage.d: Initial 10 mg once daily; if needed, increase to 20 mg once daily after 7-14 days
dosage.t: Full effect within 7-14 days; doses above 20 mg add little benefit (40 mg studied and tolerated)
dosage.n: May be combined with a diuretic or other agent

dosage.d: Instill one drop in the affected eye(s) twice daily; shake suspension well before use
dosage.t: May be used alone or with other IOP-lowering medicines (separate other drops by ~10 minutes)
dosage.n: Onset of IOP reduction within ~30 minutes

dosage.d: Severe renal impairment or dialysis: lower starting dose (e.g. 5 mg once daily), titrating in 5 mg increments
dosage.t: Betaxolol is not substantially removed by dialysis

dosage.d: Consider a lower starting dose (e.g. 5 mg once daily) and cautious titration
dosage.n: Monitor heart rate and blood pressure

admin: Oral: take once daily at the same time each day, with or without food; swallow whole
Do not discontinue oral therapy abruptly - taper over about 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound ischemia/hypertension
Ophthalmic: shake the suspension well; instill one drop into the affected eye(s) twice daily
Do not let the dropper tip touch the eye or any surface; apply nasolacrimal occlusion to reduce systemic absorption
If using other eye drops, administer them at least about 10 minutes before betaxolol
Monitor for systemic beta-blocker effects even with the ophthalmic form
moa: Betaxolol is a cardioselective beta-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist that lacks significant intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and has minimal membrane-stabilising (local anaesthetic) activity. Orally, blockade of cardiac beta-1 receptors reduces heart rate, cardiac output, and renin release, lowering blood pressure. When instilled in the eye, betaxolol reduces elevated intraocular pressure - whether or not associated with glaucoma - primarily by decreasing aqueous humour production, while having minimal effect on pupil size or accommodation. Ophthalmic betaxolol has relatively minimal effects on pulmonary and cardiovascular parameters compared with non-selective ocular beta-blockers, owing to its beta-1 selectivity.

absolute: Heart block greater than first degree (second- or third-degree AV block) without a pacemaker
Known hypersensitivity to betaxolol or any component
relative: Compensated heart failure (use cautiously with digitalis/diuretics)
Bronchospastic disease / asthma / COPD (cardioselectivity is relative and lost at higher doses)
Diabetes mellitus (may mask hypoglycaemia and impair recovery)
Thyrotoxicosis (may mask tachycardia; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate thyroid storm)
Anaesthesia / major surgery (continued or carefully managed beta-blockade)
History of severe anaphylaxis (beta-blockade may blunt response to epinephrine)
monitor: Signs and symptoms of cardiac failure

preg: Betaxolol crosses the placenta. Beta-blockers as a class may cause fetal and neonatal bradycardia, hypoglycaemia, and reduced fetal growth. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; if used near term, monitor the neonate for bradycardia and hypoglycaemia.
lact: Betaxolol is excreted in human milk. Monitor a breastfed infant for signs of beta-blockade (bradycardia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension). Use with caution and weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's need for the drug.
renal: Betaxolol is partly cleared renally. In severe renal impairment or in patients on dialysis, use a reduced oral starting dose (e.g. 5 mg once daily) and titrate cautiously by 5 mg increments. Betaxolol is not substantially removed by haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
hepatic: Betaxolol is metabolised by the liver. Use with caution in hepatic impairment; consider a lower starting oral dose and careful titration with monitoring of heart rate and blood pressure.

major: Verapamil / diltiazem and other rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers (additive bradycardia, AV block, negative inotropy)
Other negative chronotropes / antiarrhythmics - digoxin, amiodarone, clonidine (bradycardia, conduction block; clonidine withdrawal hypertension)
Catecholamine-depleting agents such as reserpine (additive hypotension and bradycardia)
moderate: Other antihypertensives and nitrates (additive blood-pressure lowering)
Insulin and oral hypoglycaemics (masked hypoglycaemia; betaxolol's beta-1 selectivity reduces but does not eliminate this)
minor: Other ophthalmic beta-blockers (avoid duplicate ocular/systemic beta-blockade)
interactions.food: Oral tablets may be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: May enhance hypotensive effect and dizziness; use moderately
interactions.diagnostics: May affect glucose tolerance tests and mask tachycardia of hypoglycaemia/hyperthyroidism

common: Ophthalmic: transient ocular discomfort/stinging, blurred vision, tearing, dry eye
serious: Bronchospasm (especially in airway disease or at higher doses)
Rebound angina / myocardial infarction / hypertension on abrupt withdrawal
rare: Worsening peripheral vascular disease / Raynaud phenomenon
emergency: Acute decompensated heart failure / pulmonary oedema
Severe symptomatic bradycardia or complete heart block
Anaphylaxis (blunted response to epinephrine while on beta-blocker)

monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure (oral therapy)
Signs/symptoms of cardiac failure (dyspnoea, oedema, weight gain)
Respiratory symptoms in patients with airway disease
Adherence and gradual tapering when stopping
counsel: Take the tablet once a day at the same time; do not stop it suddenly - your doctor will taper it to avoid heart problems
It may slow your heart rate and cause tiredness or cold hands/feet, especially at first
If you have diabetes, this medicine can hide some warning signs of low blood sugar (like a fast heartbeat) - monitor your sugars
For the eye drops: shake well, do not touch the dropper to your eye, and press gently on the inner corner of the eye for a minute to reduce body-wide effects
Report breathlessness, swelling, very slow pulse, fainting, or wheezing to your doctor
Tell any surgeon or anaesthetist that you take a beta-blocker
pk: Oral antihypertensive effect over days (full effect 7-14 days); ophthalmic IOP reduction within ~30 minutes
Oral peak plasma ~3-4 hours; ophthalmic peak IOP-lowering effect ~2 hours
Oral elimination half-life approximately 14-22 hours (supports once-daily oral dosing)
Oral: ~24 hours (once-daily dosing); ophthalmic IOP control ~12 hours (twice-daily dosing)
Store at controlled room temperature (about 20-25 degrees C); protect from light; do not freeze the ophthalmic product
pearls: Betaxolol comes in two distinct forms: ORAL tablets for hypertension and OPHTHALMIC drops for glaucoma/ocular hypertension - confirm which is intended.
It is cardioselective (beta-1) with a long half-life allowing once-daily oral dosing; selectivity is relative and diminishes at higher doses.
Never stop a beta-blocker abruptly - taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound angina, MI, or hypertension.
Ophthalmic betaxolol is absorbed systemically, so the same cardiac/respiratory cautions apply; use nasolacrimal occlusion to limit absorption.
Contraindicated in sinus bradycardia, high-degree AV block, cardiogenic shock, and overt heart failure.
Reduce the oral dose in severe renal impairment/dialysis; betaxolol is not appreciably dialysed.
missed: Oral: if you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume your once-daily schedule - do not double up. Ophthalmic: instill the missed drop when you remember, but skip it if it is nearly time for the next dose; do not use extra drops to make up.
overdose: Overdose of systemic (or substantially absorbed ophthalmic) beta-blocker may cause bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia, and acute cardiac failure. There is no specific betaxolol antidote; betaxolol is not appreciably removed by dialysis. Stop the drug and provide supportive care: gastric lavage for recent oral ingestion; atropine for bradycardia; intravenous fluids and sympathomimetic pressors (dopamine, dobutamine, or norepinephrine) for hypotension; glucagon and high-dose insulin-euglycaemia for refractory cardiac depression; bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists/aminophylline) for bronchospasm; and a transvenous pacemaker if needed. A topical ocular overdose can be flushed from the eye with warm water.
